1.title: Network Security Architecture: Segmentation, Defense in Depth and Zero Trust
1.text: Welcome to Module eleven: Network Security Architecture: Segmentation, Defense in Depth and Zero Trust. It covers the exam area four. Networking and Cloud Security Concepts. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. four point two Understand network security architecture: Comprehending network segmentation (for example firewall zones, Virtual Local Area Network (V lan), micro-segmentation). Defense in Depth. Zero Trust (Z T). Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: four. Networking and Cloud Security Concepts (twenty-one point three percent). Exam format: an adaptive exam of one hundred to one hundred twenty-five questions in two hours; a score of seven hundred on a scale of one to one thousand passes. Validated against: the official I S C two C C exam outline.

1.title: Network segmentation
1.text: Network segmentation. Segmentation divides a network into smaller zones so that a breach in one zone does not spread everywhere. It also lets you apply different rules to each zone.

1.title: Network segmentation, continued
1.text: Network segmentation. The figure shows this: A screened subnet separates the internet, the internal network and sensitive zones.

1.title: Network segmentation, continued
1.text: Network segmentation. Firewall zones. How it divides: Firewalls separate trust levels. Note: Internet, D M Z, internal, restricted. D M Z (screened subnet). How it divides: A buffer zone for public-facing servers. Note: If a web server falls, the internal network is still behind another firewall. V lan. How it divides: A logical network on shared switches. Note: Separates departments, guests, voice.

1.title: Network segmentation, continued
1.text: Network segmentation. Micro-segmentation. How it divides: Fine-grained rules around each workload or application, often in software. Note: Stops lateral movement inside a data center or cloud. Physical separation (air gap). How it divides: No connection at all. Note: Highest isolation, used for the most sensitive systems. Exam tip: Public servers go in the D M Z. A V lan separates groups; micro-segmentation protects individual workloads. Segmentation limits the blast radius.

1.title: Defense in depth
1.text: Defense in depth. Defense in depth uses several layers of different controls, so that if one fails, others still protect. No single control is trusted alone. Policies and awareness. Policies, training. Physical. Locks, badges, cameras. Perimeter. Firewalls, D M Z, email filtering. Network. Segmentation, I D S and I P S. Host or endpoint. Patching, antivirus, hardening. Application. Secure coding, waff. Data. Encryption, backups, access control. Identity. M F A, least privilege. Defense in depth combines technical, administrative and physical controls (Module four) and preventive, detective and corrective functions. Exam tip: Defense in depth equals layers. Layers should be different, because two controls of the same kind can fail the same way.

1.title: Zero trust
1.text: Zero trust. Zero trust (Z T) drops the idea that the inside of the network is trusted. No user, device or network location is trusted automatically. Never trust, always verify. Every request is authenticated and authorized. Least privilege. Minimum access, often just in time. Assume breach. Design as if an attacker is already inside; segment and monitor. Verify explicitly. Use identity, device health, location, behavior for every decision. Micro-segmentation. Small trust zones around resources. Continuous monitoring. Re-check during the session, not only at login.

1.title: Zero trust, continued
1.text: Zero trust. Strong perimeter, trusted inside. No implicit trust anywhere. Access by network location. Access by identity and context. V P N (virtual private network) gives broad access. Per-application, per-request access. A I helps by separating A I development from production data with segmentation and by spotting anomalies. Exam tip: Zero trust: never trust, always verify, assume breach, least privilege. A V P N alone is not zero trust.

1.title: Other architecture ideas
1.text: Other architecture ideas. Network access control (N A C). Checks a device before it joins (patched, approved). Honeypot. A decoy system that attracts attackers so you can study them. Bastion host or jump server. A hardened gateway for administrator access.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A company hosts a public web server and wants it separated from the internal network by a buffer zone. Which design is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: A D M Z, also called a screened subnet. A D M Z is a buffer zone for public-facing servers between the internet and the internal network.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A data center wants to stop an attacker who is already inside from moving between application servers. Which technique helps most? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Micro-segmentation with rules for each workload. Micro-segmentation applies fine-grained rules between workloads and limits lateral movement.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A company uses a firewall, M F A, encryption, endpoint protection and staff training together. Which concept is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Defense in depth, which uses many layers. Using several different layers of control is defense in depth.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Which statement best describes zero trust? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: No user or device is trusted until verified for each request. Zero trust means never trust, always verify, for every request and not only at the perimeter.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Which controls make defense in depth stronger? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Different kinds of controls at different layers. Layers should differ so that one failure mode does not defeat them all.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A guest Wi-Fi network must not reach the finance systems on the same switches. Which feature separates them? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Separate V L A Ns with firewall rules between them. V L A Ns separate groups logically, and firewall rules control any traffic between them.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What does a D M Z hold? Answer: Public-facing servers, in a buffer zone. Question two. What does segmentation limit? Answer: The spread of a breach, the blast radius. Question three. What is the core idea of zero trust? Answer: Never trust, always verify.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What does assume breach mean? Answer: Design as if an attacker is already inside. Question five. What is defense in depth? Answer: Several different layers of controls. Question six. What does a honeypot do? Answer: Attracts attackers as a decoy so they can be studied.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Segmentation: firewall zones, D M Z, V lan, micro-segmentation, air gap; limits blast radius. Defense in depth: many different layers: policy, physical, perimeter, network, host, app, data, identity. Zero trust: never trust, always verify; least privilege; assume breach; continuous monitoring. Extras: N A C, honeypot, jump server.
